That comeback has a history, and it's older than me by a lot. In 1972 James P. Anderson's planning
study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor: a piece every access has to pass through,
that can't be tampered with, and small enough to check. In 2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued that a monitor that only watches a
run as it goes can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at some finite point, the kind
computer scientists call safety rules. ``No certificate without an
earlier passing check and a commit'' is one of those. And in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim, a computer scientist then at the University of Pennsylvania, and six
coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single instruction, and proved them correct in
Coq. So putting a rule under every program, so nothing can
get around it, is their move. I didn't invent it. What I'm putting under that move is narrower: a record that
has to be paid for, on the small machine one that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting,
why a finite machine that prices its merges can't make the price of a record that never comes down zero.

before:
Which of the proved part is new? Not one big thing, and I'd be suspicious of me if I said otherwise.
By my own sorting at the back (Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}) it's four smaller ones, each with its
neighbours standing right there. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on
merging: the pigeonhole principle, Landauer and Bennett on merging, and the finite heart of
the German mathematician Ernst Zermelo's 1896 recurrence argument, about whether a closed box of gas has to come back around to where it started, are all next to it. A window that shows a certifying step and a
quiet one alike, before
and after, can't price certification exactly: an old fact about functions, the
1956 thought experiments of Edward Moore, at Bell Labs, on what you can learn about a machine you
may only watch from outside, and the engineer Rudolf Kalman's observability, the same question
asked of control systems. What I put in is a price. A base-driven permanent record, over
any machine, is a latch on one event: the 1918 flip-flop and write-once memory are its neighbours.
And the small machine, a definition of Thiele-complete that a clock can't meet, and a universal
Thiele machine written as one fixed program: a record that's priced, and earned, under the reference
monitor's every-program move (Anderson in 1972, Schneider in 2000, Coq-checked monitors from Azevedo
de Amorim and coauthors in 2015), carried to every program of the small machine and, with one paid
move added, to every computably presented Thiele machine. That fourth one is built and checked;
the idea under it isn't new. The first three are small exact statements I didn't find stated before, where I looked. The
two-player game check later in the book is careful engineering on known mathematics. It doesn't make a fifth.

And the stuff from the start, the audit, the proof, the ledger, the test sheet, the sticker, the
confident AI? Here's the straight answer on which of those this helps. The sticker is a question of whether a piece of paper is
genuine, and nothing here touches it. The ``all tests passed'' sheet fits only if the test is a
checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine's own language; a set of tests that can miss a
bug certifies ``this procedure said yes,'' which is true and smaller. An audit and a ledger get the
test sheet's answer: kept by a program on an ordinary computer, they're bits the program wrote, and
they fit only where the step underneath keeps the record and refuses to raise it without the check.
A proof is the case this book is built on. A proof checked by a proof assistant is a check that could
have said no, and the checker vouches that the proof fits its statement; whether the statement says
what you meant is still yours to read. The AI that talks as if it's sure of
itself isn't addressed at all. What the book gives you is a record on the machine itself, with a
proof of what a raised one means. Getting that record to somebody across the room who has to
believe it is a separate job, and Section~\ref{sec:scope}, under ``Outward consequences,'' says how
little of the outside world I've reached. If you came for a tool, that's a short list. If you came
for the question, this is where it starts.

before:
\emph{Substrate versus scaffolding.} Two layers run through the book, and confusing them makes
the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The \emph{substrate} is the shape: a kind of
state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different extra pieces,
and the pieces aren't the same. The universal floor (the ``pays something'' result above)
asks for a certification reading and the toll on it. The counter's uniqueness (only one
count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a schedule of
increments; Part III gives the argument, a short induction that works for any system with
those two pieces, and on the small machine of Part IV the ledger is the sum of the charges by
theorem (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). The diagonal asks for a way to write programs as states and a recursion theorem for
the transformations the substrate can express, and needs no toll at all. ``Substrate-level''
doesn't mean one fixed plug that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts
it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it'll tell you, and whatever else is lying around the
workshop isn't the theorem's. So each result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I
mean by \emph{the model}, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The \emph{scaffolding} is
everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say \emph{my machine}, \emph{the
small machine}, \emph{the machine I build} or \emph{the build}, this is what I mean: the machine
of Part IV, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked facts, its channel,
trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction kinds and their prices, the host with a register for every
whole number, the universal programs that run on that host, and the Coq files that define all of
it. The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows, for any one theorem, only
the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and a theorem stated over one extension
starts reading as if it carried premises it never uses. ``Substrate'' never means the build,
and it never means the side of a simulation doing the stepping; for that I say ``the machine
doing the stepping,'' as against ``the program it runs.''

Part IV has one piece of scaffolding, and I'd rather you know up front how small it is.
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six
instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there
(a flag raised from a clean start was
checked, then committed, then certified, on the same
edition, with nothing touching
that thing between the check and the commit), and so is universality, through Minsky's two-counter machines and a halting result
borrowed from the Coq undecidability library. Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same
kinds of instruction with more counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move added,
every computably presented Thiele machine. None of that is the model. It shows the model fits in
six instruction kinds.

before:
\begin{itemize}
\item Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up. It
constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the model's step
function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
\item Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the smallest
trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine's semantics. Here no proof rides along with
the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
\item Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the conversation
can't go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid to establish.
Different problem.
\item No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem, whatever an
optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That's an average over a whole
problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The toll charges one step in one run,
with no refund anywhere.
\item Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the structure in an object is the length of the
shortest program that prints it. That's a property of a finished string, with no steps and
no moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
\item Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding looks
expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP question, a gap in
how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor under the one step that
commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
\item The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at temperature
T gives off at least kT ln 2. That's the closest thing to the toll itself I've found, because it
charges a commitment. An object or an average isn't what it prices. But it's physics, indexed to a
temperature, and its choice is unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where
the toll's commit is a deterministic merge that stays. The toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no
temperature in it. Closest neighbour. A different chair.
\item Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten Wolde 2017):
making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the two come apart has a
thermodynamic bill. The nearest physics I've found to ``learning free, committing priced.'' It's
heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the toll is a count in a model of computation.
\item Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the smallest automaton
for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising that language on a
device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if the smallest automaton only
reshuffles, recognition can be free. That's the chairs with a physical price on them, and one
of their worked examples is the latch's language turned inside out. It's the closest neighbour
of all to the road the toll is derived on; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says exactly
what's left over for me.
\item CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified C compiler that carries the object
code's execution cost back up to annotations on the source. There the cost decorates the
program and survives compilation. Here it lives in the model's step rule.
\item Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000; Azevedo de
Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes through, enforcing a rule on
every program. Schneider argued that a monitor watching a run can enforce only rules whose
breaking shows up at a finite point, and ``no certificate without an earlier passing check and
commit'' is one of those; the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved in
Coq. That's the move the small machine's step makes, so this one is the house itself. What's added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record on top,
and the derivation of why the payment can't be zero. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and Fred
Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors, program rewriters and static checkers can
each enforce, and they differ, which is one reason this book doesn't claim that every enforcement
mechanism is a Thiele machine underneath.
\item Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and coauthors
2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022; Clement, Junqueira, Kate and
Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica that a replica taken over still can't make
say two things, with a proof of exactly what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn't in
their picture.
\item Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014): variables
added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the program computes. The flag and
the counter are ghost in that sense. The small machine's table of checked facts isn't, because
the step reads it and refuses on it, for every program.
\item Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and Raykova 2013;
Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger, that a computation's output is
right. That establishes the claim for the stranger, and anyone with the inputs can make one,
the copier included. The record here is about one machine's own history. A proof like that is
one way to carry the local record out of the box.
\item Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking who is
committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom's entitlements can be defeated and can be
passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step by step, and a copy carries it only as
far as the copy is genuine. Same words, different machinery.
\item Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In protocol
verification, ``this end event must be preceded by a begin event for the same thing'' is a
correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove a protocol keeps it against any
opponent. ``No certificate without an earlier commit, and no commit without an earlier check
of the same claim'' has that shape. Theirs is proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced
by the step, which is the LCF comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
\item Monotonic parallel composition (\AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persistence in the
pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). \AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow
separate models where a neighbouring process can never stop a step from models that can solve
consensus, and test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what was there, is
on the consensus side. Palamidessi and coauthors compare messages that are used up with
messages that stay, and the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. The small
machine, put into \AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow's setting with threads pooled on one shared state,
has a consensus process in their sense, so it lands on their non-monotonic side; that, and their
theorem, are checked. The
comparison with Palamidessi and coauthors' persistence stays a comparison.
\item Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral and
coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device that runs in a
cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse isn't. It's the nearest
physics I know to ``committing costs'' stated for a cycling device. It's quantum and
approximate, and the chairs are classical, finite and exact
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).
\item Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; K\"usters, Truderung
and Vogt 2010; Treitz and K\"unnemann 2026): when an outside party can tell who misbehaved.
Their windows are this book's windows, and the trust they leave over, an honest log or a
trusted step, is left over here too (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\item Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone you don't
trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof doesn't. That's the argument
for carrying the object and re-running the check (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\end{itemize}

temperature, and its choice is unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where
the toll's commit is a deterministic merge that stays. The toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no
temperature in it. Closest neighbour. A different chair.
\item Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten Wolde 2017):
making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the two come apart has a
thermodynamic bill. The nearest physics I've found to ``learning free, committing priced.'' It's
heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the toll is a count in a model of computation.
\item Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the smallest automaton
for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising that language on a
device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if the smallest automaton only
reshuffles, recognition can be free. That's the chairs with a physical price on them, and one
of their worked examples is the latch's language turned inside out. It's the closest neighbour
of all to the road the toll is derived on; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says exactly
what's left over for me.
\item CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified C compiler that carries the object
code's execution cost back up to annotations on the source. There the cost decorates the
program and survives compilation. Here it lives in the model's step rule.
\item Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000; Azevedo de
Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes through, enforcing a rule on
every program. Schneider argued that a monitor watching a run can enforce only rules whose
breaking shows up at a finite point, and ``no certificate without an earlier passing check and
commit'' is one of those; the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved correct. That's the move the small machine's step makes, so this one is the house itself. What's added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record on top,
and the derivation of why the payment can't be zero. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and Fred
Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors, program rewriters and static checkers can
each enforce, and they differ, which is one reason this book doesn't claim that every enforcement
mechanism is a Thiele machine underneath.
\item Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and coauthors
2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022; Clement, Junqueira, Kate and
Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica that a replica taken over still can't make
say two things, with a proof of exactly what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn't in
their picture.
\item Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014): variables
added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the program computes. The flag and
the counter are ghost in that sense. The small machine's table of checked facts isn't, because
the step reads it and refuses on it, for every program.
\item Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and Raykova 2013;
Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger, that a computation's output is
right. That establishes the claim for the stranger, and anyone with the inputs can make one,
the copier included. The record here is about one machine's own history. A proof like that is
one way to carry the local record out of the box.
\item Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking who is
committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom's entitlements can be defeated and can be
passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step by step, and a copy carries it only as
far as the copy is genuine. Same words, different machinery.
\item Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In protocol
verification, ``this end event must be preceded by a begin event for the same thing'' is a
correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove a protocol keeps it against any
opponent. ``No certificate without an earlier commit, and no commit without an earlier check
of the same claim'' has that shape. Theirs is proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced
by the step, which is the LCF comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
\item Monotonic parallel composition (\AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persistence in the
pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). \AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow
separate models where a neighbouring process can never stop a step from models that can solve
consensus, and test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what was there, is
on the consensus side. Palamidessi and coauthors compare messages that are used up with
messages that stay, and the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. The small
machine, put into \AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow's setting with threads pooled on one shared state,
has a consensus process in their sense, so it lands on their non-monotonic side; that, and their
theorem, are checked. The
comparison with Palamidessi and coauthors' persistence stays a comparison.
\item Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral and
coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device that runs in a
cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse isn't. It's the nearest
physics I know to ``committing costs'' stated for a cycling device. It's quantum and
approximate, and the chairs are classical, finite and exact
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).
\item Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; K\"usters, Truderung
and Vogt 2010; Treitz and K\"unnemann 2026): when an outside party can tell who misbehaved.
Their windows are this book's windows, and the trust they leave over, an honest log or a
trusted step, is left over here too (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\item Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone you don't
trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof doesn't. That's the argument
for carrying the object and re-running the check (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\end{itemize}

before: What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the code. Not one line of it. By the time the Coq proofs finally landed, every line of that first renderer had been thrown out and rewritten at least twice, probably more, and good riddance to all of it. What survived was a single architectural commitment I made early and never once let anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the actual thing the machine runs on. It is no metaphor laid over some realer state underneath. Category theory was the first language I found for that structure. It is not what the model is. The model asks for a state, a step, a record, a ledger, and a window, and category theory appears nowhere in that list. It lived on for a while in a bigger machine I built on the way here, a fifty-one-instruction virtual machine with its own chip design, whose partition graph (groups, and arrows between them) was, in different words and different syntax, the same object as the category structure that came together in that first week and first ran morphisms correctly at two in the morning. That machine was useful for building and confusing for everything else, so it's set aside now, kept but out of this book. What building it showed me is that six instruction kinds were enough for everything this book needs, and that the big one was mostly in the way. I did not write that code, not then and not now. I directed the models and refused everything they handed me until the morphisms composed the way the shape said they had to. The morphisms in that early code were objects that remembered where they came from; the records in the small machine I ended up with remember where they came from too, and you can walk up to one and challenge it. The receipt grew teeth. But the shape itself never moved. The shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything else, every renderer and language and proof, was me slowly learning to see what I had already built. By the shape I mean structure held as state. Not category theory. Category theory was just the first language I had for it.

before: Formal verification was a graveyard of dead ends further on. The hardware came after that, in the bigger machine I set aside, and none of it is in this book. Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known was there, and I mean that plainly: I did not know what a Turing machine was when I started, I did not know what Coq was, I did not know most of the words in this document existed. The learning came after, dragged along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.

before: Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want the division of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong about work like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference implementation, no prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the direction, the demand that the thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk. The symbol-pushing, the code and the formal derivations, the models produced. I used the checker to catch gaps in those derivations. Coq is an obedient idiot. It checks the proof matches the statement. It does not check that the statement means what you think it means. A theorem can claim ``every cat that is also a prime number has whiskers'' and the proof can be three characters long and Coq will nod and stamp it. So I read every statement. An accepted derivation can still settle an empty question. I had to refuse that too. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable by reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had typed it. The monkeys could not have refused.

before:
Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine's whole state is the strip.
Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any box has a 1 in
it.
Check the three premises. Permanent: once there's a 1, there's always a 1. Flip: the empty
strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. Forgets nothing: every move can be undone by
erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become the same strip. So here is a machine
that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges anything. The room argument has no grip on
it, and the toll doesn't follow. The checked version is \code{unbounded\_history\_escapes}, and its
state is a list of bits of any length, which is the formal way of saying the strip has no end.

before:
Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is undoable
(turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads: that's a flip, NO to YES.
And heads goes to tails: the same move takes the flag back down somewhere else. Two states,
finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets nothing, so a schedule that
charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing. The file states that the one move
forgets nothing
(it is injective) and its on-then-off behaviour; that the coin is
finite and that the price may be zero are written in \code{toggle\_escape}, which
prices the turn at zero, meets merge pricing, and fails the toll.
The thing that walked out the door is permanence.

blank and one stamped. One move: stamp whatever you're handed. Finite, two states.

up for nothing.

about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges \emph{every} forgetting move,
whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer's own heat, as the coin under
the cup below will show, is owed only for what you didn't know. So the premise is Landauer's
claim taken in its worst case over what the machine might be holding, and that's the
version the counting needs.

A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step. For such a run, the
adopted entropy-loss premise reduces to $Q \ge 0$: it supplies no positive heat lower bound.
That does not establish that a particular device attains zero heat. The chairs guarantee a
collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-state. They do not
guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision (a four-state machine where it
doesn't is \code{nec\_f\_collision\_avoids\_s}, NecFMerge.v). For an input distribution
supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone therefore forces no positive entropy
loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends on the move. The operation-level
ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.

adopted entropy-loss premise reduces to $Q \ge 0$: it supplies no positive heat lower bound.
That does not establish that a particular device attains zero heat. The chairs guarantee a
collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-state. They do not
guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision (take four states $s,a,b,c$, with only $s$ reading no, and a move
$s\mapsto a$, $a\mapsto b$, $b\mapsto b$, $c\mapsto c$). For an input distribution
supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone therefore forces no positive entropy
loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends on the move. The operation-level
ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.

One piece of it I can hand you. Take
one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states that run passes through are
finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it would
be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every one of them back around, the start
included, where the flag was down. So if the flag goes up along that run and stays up from
some point on, the move merges two states \emph{the run itself visits}. The shared chair is
one the machine actually sits in. And it doesn't touch the known-state point above: a merge
among states the run visits still costs Landauer nothing if the run knew where it was and
something outside timed the step. Checked as \code{nec\_f\_orbit\_merges\_visited} and
\code{nec\_f\_repeat\_merges\_visited}, for any map iterated from a start whose flag
is down, with the flag up at every step from some point on; no permanence premise is used.

Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to give here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at
all, the answer is no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. Move $a$ swaps them;
move $b$ does nothing. Run $a$ once and then $b$ forever: the flag goes up at the first step and
stays up for good, and neither move merges anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down
from the yes-state if it ever ran there; on this run it never does, and that's exactly the
weakened permanence this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next
move from its own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it
stands. Now say the moves come in a
pattern that eventually repeats, one word $w$ of moves over and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the
repeating starts, and goes up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was down (start
$w$ at that letter if you have to) and run the same argument on the composite of $w$'s moves, at the states where such a repetition begins. It merges two
of those states, both visited; follow the two through the letters of $w$, and the first letter
where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that letter's place in the pattern.
So: moves picked from outside, no; a closed machine or a repeating program, yes
(\code{nec\_f\_outside\_moves\_no\_merge}, \code{nec\_f\_closed\_merges\_visited} and
\code{nec\_f\_word\_merges\_visited}, NecFRepeat.v; the last finds the letter and the two
repetitions, from a flag down at the start and up at every repetition from some point on).

Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it gets
interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a machine in the
same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there's no single place
to send that state. That's the whole obstruction, and it's exact: the map from states exists
on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come from lists that agree on the
other side. Call that the \emph{descent} condition, because it's what
lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll doesn't force it. Take the one-bit machine whose set costs one and whose
reset is free. It obeys the toll, yet a single set and a reset followed by a set leave its
bit in the same state. A target that keeps its whole history as its state tells those two
runs apart, so nothing comes down. So the fold is unique on lists, and that's what the word ``initial''
earns. It doesn't make anybody's states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I
won't say it does. The fold and the descent condition are checked over any machine: the fold
is the one such map, descent holds exactly when each reachable
state goes to one target state, and a map the fold
factors through gives descent, all in NecFCounter.v; the
history-keeping machine is the example that shows where descent fails
.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it's up. A step from
down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step's cost plus potential change to be
non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That's the toll, exactly, and the two are the
same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step has non-negative
amortized cost under the flag potential (``amortized cost'' is just that sum, the step's cost
plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, ``any run from NO to YES
paid at least one,'' is just the potential method's standard conclusion, the drop in
potential from one to zero, and every system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an
instance (the checked record carries the toll as a field, so that's every certification
system). Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag
at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a unit and a unit isn't used
twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too, that the potential before a step covers
its cost plus the potential after, then the two together hold exactly when raising the flag
costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and the flag never comes down; that's the
sharpest version of
the schedule, and notice that Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toy doesn't meet it: the toy's VOUCH move, played from
YES, makes a mark
although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact version forbids. (These
two theorems let the price depend on the state as well as the move's name, which is wider
than Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a special case.) Two older tools sit beside
these, named for completeness: running a list of moves in a ``writer'' that accumulates a
number returns the final state and the run's cost, and a
per-move schedule is a ``grade'' fixed before the run; neither
embeds those frameworks' full type systems, and the files say so. The writer is the move
the programming-language researchers Norman Danner and Daniel Licata make in their cost semantics, a translation that carries a cost alongside
a program's result (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015; Danner and Licata, \emph{Journal of
Functional Programming}, 2022). The grade is Shin-ya Katsumata's: a computation carries its resource
as a grade, and the grades compose as the computations do (``Parametric effect monads and
semantics of effect systems,'' POPL 2014). Dominic Orchard, Vilem Liepelt and Harley Eades put grades into the
types of a working language (``Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal types,'' ICFP
2019). And the potential method went into types before any of those: the computer scientists
Martin Hofmann and Steffen Jost (POPL 2003) gave a type system that attaches potential to data and
predicts, before a first-order functional program runs, how much heap it can use, which is where
type-based amortized analysis begins; the multivariate work of Jan Hoffmann, Klaus Aehlig and
Hofmann (2011) carried it further. Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step rule. No type
carries it. And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a type gets checked
before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that lives in the state gets
written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different moment of truth.

How close do the two moments come? Close enough to say exactly, in a limited form. Take a small structured language over a machine with this kind of counter:
sequencing, branches whose two arms carry the same grade, and paid acts each graded with their
charge, and grade every program the way Katsumata's discipline does, adding grades along the
program. On loop-free programs the two agree on the nose: on every run that doesn't trap, the
counter rises by exactly the grade. The argument is conservation set beside the grade rule; the
counter's rise is the sum of the charges along the run, and the grade rule adds the same charges
in the same order. Loops break the agreement, and in one direction only. A loop that runs a
paid
check once for every unit
in some register, where the check
always
passes and is charged one,
costs that register's value on
entry, and no fixed whole number is an exact grade for it; a grade that's a function of the
inputs, the kind cost-aware type theories like calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022)
allow, gets exactness back. So the counter carries their semantics exactly, agrees with fixed
grades wherever a fixed grade can be exact, and where a run's cost depends on its data it holds
the exact number that a fixed grade can only bound. Checked as \code{nec\_f\_grade\_exact}, with
the small machine as an instance in \code{nec\_f\_grade\_exact\_small}, and for the loop
\code{nec\_f\_loop\_cost}, \code{nec\_f\_loop\_no\_fixed\_grade} and \code{nec\_f\_loop\_input\_grade}
. What has no counterpart in the step is the
checking ahead of time: a type checker turning a program away before it runs.

Not if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot. Here's why, and it's the cube again.
Suppose there are
two steps that give the clerk the same before-photo and the same after-photo, and one of them
raised the flag and the other didn't. (The two-move toy above is exactly such a pair; so are
``a stamp goes onto a document inside a closed drawer'' and ``someone opens and closes the
drawer.'') The clerk has one bill for that pair of photographs. If the bill is at least one,
it overcharges the step that didn't raise the flag. If it's zero, it undercharges the step
that did. Any bill that never misses a raise bills something that wasn't a raise, and no
bill from those photographs is exact. The fix is the plain one: put the flag in the
photograph. If the window shows the reading, then ``one when the reading goes from down to
up, zero otherwise'' is exact, and such a window has no pair like the one above. That's enough.
It isn't the only way: a window can hide the flag and still have no colliding pair, in
which case a bill from the photographs can be exact; what ShadowPricing.v proves the other way is
only that a colliding pair rules exact pricing out. And ``exact'' here means rise-only pricing: at least
one on every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn't. That's all the
clerk's problem needs, and the bill ``one for a raise, zero otherwise'' meets it
. So it's exact about \emph{which} steps get charged. It isn't exact about \emph{how much}, and it
doesn't pick out one bill: ``two for a raise, zero
otherwise'' meets it too. Pinning the bill down takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any
run, the total never exceeds the number of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there's
exactly one bill left, one per raise and zero otherwise; that's an if and only if, proved for
any system whose bill is decided step by step. These are stated for any states and any steps. The window version, the cube theorem with a
price in place of a decoder, comes next.

\begin{definition}[Entitlement]\label{def:u08-entitlement}
A run is \emph{entitled} to a claim when three things are on hand: an \emph{object} carried in the run's
states; a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the claim, meaning a test that was run
and whose result is on the record; and a \emph{paid event}, a move of the run at which
the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least one. In a certification
system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) a move that takes the reading from no to yes is such a
move, because the toll charges it. This is the book's word; there's no Coq definition of it.
\end{definition}

People got here before me, and from a direction I didn't expect, which was programming for many
processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton's LVars (2013), ``lattice-based data structures
for deterministic parallelism'' in their own title, are memory cells whose value only climbs in an
order, where a read can't ask for the value and can only ask whether it has climbed past a
threshold. That's a cup. What the cup buys them took me a couple of reads. As I understand it,
writers running side by side can push the value up in a different order on every run, and a cup
that's up stays up whatever the order was, so a program that only ever looks at cups can't see
the others' timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs about programs,
show in Coq, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried as monotone ghost state
in a program logic. That's the closest thing I've found to the decomposition into lines being
checked by somebody else. The match is my reading, and if it's off, that's on me.

Here's what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this book that
computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church's, from the 1930s, and it's
a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A term is one of three things. A
variable. A function, written $\lambda$ followed by its body, the body saying what to do with
whatever you hand it. Or one term applied to another, written side by side. Running a program
is one move, over and over: when a function meets an argument, put the argument into the body
where the variable was. No numbers, no memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published a proof that
it computes exactly what his machines compute. ``Weak call-by-value'' is two house rules about
the order of moves: an argument is run down to a finished function (a \emph{value}) before it's
put in, and nothing runs inside a function that hasn't been handed anything yet. Variables
are written as numbers counting how many $\lambda$s back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas
de Bruijn, who ran the Automath proof-checking project at Eindhoven from 1967 and comes back in
Section~\ref{sec:coq}; it means two variables can never get mixed up by sharing a name), and a term is \emph{closed}
when every variable in it is bound inside it, so it leans on nothing outside. Last piece: to
hand a program to a program, L needs a way to write any term as data, the way a program's
source is a string you can pass around. The one used here is the \emph{Scott encoding}, named for
Dana Scott, a student of Church's who went on to build mathematical models of the lambda calculus
itself. As far as I can trace it, the encoding first appeared in lecture notes of his from Berkeley
in 1962 that he never published. All you need about it is that every term $t$ gets one \emph{code}, written
$\ulcorner t \urcorner$, and the code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of
that in the proof: a \emph{quoting} term $Q$ that takes the code of a term to the code of that
code (a program that prints its own source needs exactly this move), and a \emph{fixed-point
combinator}, a term that lets a function call itself, which is how $Q$ works its way through
a code of any size.

more. Not the system. I'll say for each one what the fragment is and what it isn't, because
``Ethereum has been formalised'' is the kind of sentence that gets a book thrown across a
room, and rightly.

The fragment: a transcription of a published Coq proof of Casper's accountable safety
(the casper-proofs development from Runtime Verification and the University of Texas at
Austin, itself based on Yoichi Hirai's proof in Isabelle, another proof checker; proofs redone on the standard library), with validator sets as predicates and
quorum intersection as a premise. A \emph{quorum} is a set of validators big enough to act, here
two thirds of the stake, and \emph{quorum intersection} is the arithmetic of the three-validator
example: two thirds plus two thirds is four thirds, so any two quorums share at least a
third. The fragment takes the overlap as given. It doesn't do that arithmetic. No deposits,
no rewards, no fork choice (the rule for picking a branch to build on), no connection to
anything else in this book. \code{accountable\_safety}: a finalization fork implies that a set of
validators the size of that overlap, at least a third of the stake, is slashed. And
\code{finalization\_without\_slashing}: a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody's slashed, which
is the ``write is free'' sentence in a degenerate setting, and only there.

The obvious question to ask of all that is whether the toll is the only way. A theorem saying so
would be the best thing this book could hold: a short list of requirements that any account of
what a step costs has to meet, whatever field it comes from, with the toll and the counter the
only accounting left standing. I looked for that theorem, and the answer I can give you is no, and
the no is small enough to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and
twice reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are. The
smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth forgets something, so
the price on merging from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} charges it a mark. It raises nothing, so the toll
leaves it free. Now try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes
nothing, none on a move that forgets nothing, the same bill when you rename the states, a total
that adds up along a run, a bill that looks only at the step, and one mark on the flip from blank. The toll, read as
the bill that charges the flip from blank and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine.
So does the price on merging. They disagree on the
smooth, so that list doesn't pick between them. What picks the toll is a requirement that names
the record: over any run the total is never more than the number of times the reading went up.
With the floor, that leaves exactly one bill, one mark per raise and nothing else
(Section~\ref{sec:windows}), and it rules the price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price a
mark and raises nothing. All of that is checked on the three states: \code{nec\_f\_three\_toll\_meets},
\code{nec\_f\_three\_merge\_meets}, \code{nec\_f\_three\_bills\_differ},
\code{nec\_f\_three\_ceiling\_picks\_toll} and \code{nec\_f\_three\_merge\_fails\_ceiling}, with the
general uniqueness as \code{nec\_f\_record\_ceiling\_unique}. The only renaming
of the three states that respects the moves is the identity,
so the renaming requirement asks nothing there. So the uniqueness is real and it's small. It holds once you've said which
reading you're charging for, and which reading deserves the charge is the pointer thesis,
which is still a thesis.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation sits and
how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this chapter's
machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus one and a jump,
then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power in through some instruction
I made fancy. For this construction I can reuse the two-counter result in the Coq Library of
Undecidability Proofs. The halting reduction is their work; the step-for-step connection
to this machine is the part I have to establish.

before:
Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes \AA{}man Pohjola and
Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow is one of the inventors of the
pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that talk over channels), in 2016 proved, with the
proof checked in the Isabelle proof assistant, that no model whose parallel composition is
monotonic, where a neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus process. One of
their examples of a model that does is test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports
what was there. Test-and-set isn't a sticky bit: in Herlihy's ranking it brings two processors to
agree, and a sticky bit brings any number.

Now the part that isn't mine. Proving that halting is undecidable for two-counter machines
is real work, and it's already done, checked, in a shared Coq project called the Coq
Library of Undecidability Proofs (presented by Yannick Forster, Dominique Larchey-Wendling
and coauthors at CoqPL 2020). The two-counter result in it is Larchey-Wendling's, reached
from his and Forster's work on Minsky machines (CPP 2019) by way of FRACTRAN, a model of computation invented by John Conway, the English mathematician best known for the Game of Life, which the library uses as a stepping stone. Their two-counter machine has the
same two instructions as Minsky's, with the same rule for zero. Andrej Dudenhefner, one of the
library's authors, writes that rule out in his 2022 paper on deciding questions about
two-counter machines: DEC on a counter at zero goes on to the next instruction, and otherwise
it takes one off the counter and jumps. So the only thing I have to
prove is that their machine and my INC/DEC fragment are the same machine, step for step,
and then borrow their theorem.

before:
One honest wrinkle about what ``undecidable'' means in that library, because it isn't the
textbook sentence. Every function you can write in Coq is a program, so in that library
``decidable'' means ``some Coq function answers it.'' Coq by itself can't prove that \emph{no} Coq function
answers a question without an extra assumption about what programs are. So the library
says the strongest thing it can without one: if anything decided this, then the questions
on which a single-tape Turing machine \emph{doesn't} halt could be listed by a program, which is
the classic thing that can't be done. That's their convention, and the theorem below
inherits it exactly.
after:
Be precise about the reduction used below. A procedure deciding this halting question
would give a program listing the single-tape Turing machines that do not halt. Such a
listing cannot exist: halting runs can already be listed, and running the two listings
in parallel would decide halting. The undecidability statement below records that
reduction, so its meaning is in the connection between the two problems.

The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous wording isn't
about what you'd guess. ``Who will guard the guardians?'' gets quoted about governments and police
and, lately, proof assistants. Where's it from? Plato's
\emph{Republic} has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e), Glaucon, Plato's older brother and
one of the people Socrates is talking with, says it would be absurd for a guardian
to need a guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man calling the question
silly. The Latin, \emph{quis custodiet ipsos custodes}, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal's sixth
satire, and it's a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set guards
on her; the line asks who'll watch the guards, since she'll start with them. And it gets better.
In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of that satire in a medieval
manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies lack, partly overlapping the familiar
ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle. Scholars have argued ever since about whether
those lines are Juvenal's at all. So the most quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes
with a doubtful source of its own. Does that change anything here? No. The only answer I know
that works is de Bruijn's (Section~\ref{sec:coq} has it): you never get rid of the last guard, you
make the last guard small enough to watch yourself. Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval} is one line per
property. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates you can hold in your head, and everything else
meant to follow from them.

The closest earlier result is in capability hardware, and it's much bigger. The computer
scientists Jack Dennis and Earl Van Horn, at MIT, introduced \emph{capabilities} in 1966: tokens a
process has to hold to touch an object, which it can pass on and can't forge. CHERI, a
capability extension of real instruction sets built at the University of Cambridge and SRI
International, rests on that idea, and in 2020 Kyndylan Nienhuis and twelve coauthors proved in the
proof checker Isabelle/HOL, for the whole CHERI-MIPS instruction set, that arbitrary code given
some capabilities can't increase them as it runs (up to any change of protection domain). That's
nothing gets forged across a full instruction set. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-forging} is the same
shape, one instruction at a time, for six instruction kinds and a table of checked facts.

Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first universal machine had
bugs. It's the machine in Turing's 1936 paper, and nobody gets to call Turing careless. In 1947
Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem of Thue, pointed out that the construction
leaned on a convention it hadn't earned, and he patched a small defect in how the universal
machine writes out each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined
the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer, worked through
the universal machine's tables and found more mistakes, much to Turing's annoyance, as the
accounts of Davies's life have it. (It's the same Davies who later named the
\emph{packet} in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in a collection edited by
Jack Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing who runs an archive of Turing's papers,
\emph{The Essential Turing}, in 2004. They may be some of the first bugs
ever written, in a program for a computer that didn't exist yet. That's a lovely claim and a
hard one to check, so take it as a lead. I can't give it to you as a fact. What it changes here: a universal machine
is exactly the kind of construction where a careful person leaves a hole, $U$ has 3728 lines for
a hole to hide in, and its theorems are checked by Coq one case at a time, which is the kind of
check that catches Davies's kind of slip. It doesn't catch a definition that says the wrong
thing. That's why the definitions are on the page, for you.

A fixed checker that runs whatever program it's handed and always answers needs saying how, so
here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number $r$. The checker decodes $r$
as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they sit, which register holds the
answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many registers to load. If $r$ doesn't decode to a
routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the checker loads the routine's registers from $v$, reads a
fuel number $f$ out of $v$ too (the fuel register's entry in $v$'s prime factorisation), runs the
routine for at most $f$ steps, and says yes exactly when by then the routine has left its code
with 1 in its answer register. Every input gets an answer within $f$ steps, so the checker is
total, and what it means is that bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the
fuel the value carries, with answer 1 (\code{cg\_ueval\_total} and \code{cg\_ueval\_iff},
CompilerChecker.v, through the host's one property \code{pu\_heval}, UniversalPCodes.v). That's
how it stays clear of the diagonal. A total evaluator $E$ that agreed with every total yes-or-no
program on that program's code alone would let $g(n) = \neg E(n, n)$ contradict itself at its own
code. This checker never evaluates a program on its code alone: the fuel comes with the claim's
value. The guest compiled from $M$ runs $M$'s reading routine itself and puts at least the step
count it took into the fuel register, and at such a value the checker says yes if and only if the
reading says yes.

\begin{definition}[The host]\label{def:u34-host}
A \emph{guest} is a program $P$ of this chapter's machine together with a state $g$ of it
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}). A \emph{host state} $h$ has six parts: its own core
$\mathrm{core}(h)$, its ledger $\mu(h)$, its own flag $\mathrm{own}(h)$, the guest program
$P(h)$ held as a list of instructions, the guest state $g(h)$, and the \emph{mirror} $m(h)$, a
yes/no copy of the guest's flag. The host has two kinds of move. $\mathrm{OWN}\ i$ runs the
instruction $i$ on the host's own core, costs what this chapter's machine charges for $i$,
and raises $\mathrm{own}$ exactly when that machine's flag would rise. $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$
costs $b$. If the host's core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to
its next line and, if the guest's next instruction costs at most $b$, runs that instruction
on $g(h)$; in the same move the mirror becomes $m(h) \lor (\lnot\mathrm{cert}(g(h)) \land
\mathrm{cert}(g'))$, where $g'$ is the new guest state. The host's reading is
$\mathrm{own}(h) \lor m(h)$. Its stored program is $U_0 = [\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1;\ \mathrm{OWN}\
(\text{INC } A);\ \mathrm{OWN}\ (\text{DEC } A\ 1)]$: one guest step, then two moves that
bring the host back to its first line. (The Coq file calls it \code{U}; I write $U_0$ here so
nobody mixes it up with the universal program $U$.)
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
(1) The prefix writes register 2 $c$ times and nothing else, so it moves that register's version from
0 to $c$. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later version of register 2, and the
version in every fact the run records about register 2, is $c$ more than in a clean run. A CHECK or a
COMMIT reads versions only to ask whether two versions of the same register are equal, and adding $c$
to both keeps the answer, so the two runs take the same steps. The run is $V$'s run from the stated
start, moved down by $c$ lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number into a program, runs it step by
step on given registers, and, searching over the number of steps, returns the output of the first
halting run. I wrote that algorithm out in Coq, turned it into a term of the lambda calculus L, and
ran the library's compiler from L to Minsky programs, which gives a program of two-counter
instructions that a host program can be read off from, instruction for instruction. The tools
supply the program that computes the evaluator. The fixed-point argument below is not theirs.
\end{proof}

So Part IV has one machine, and it isn't the model. It's a Thiele machine in the front matter's
sense, an instance of the certification system with the toll proved: \code{earned\_cs}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-instance}). It's Thiele-complete, in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}, the sense no clock meets
(Observation~\ref{thm:u34-clock} and Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-instances}): it computes whatever a Turing
machine can, under Minsky's $2^n$ encoding, done outside the machine, its computing is free and can't touch the record, and, from a clean start, its record is earned. And the
universal Thiele machine runs on a host made of its own kinds of instruction: one fixed program,

programming language. It calls that \emph{extraction}. In the drawings every part comes wearing a
coat of proof, and extraction takes the coat off: the proof parts are thrown away and what's left is

programming language that Coq's extraction supports directly. Two files do it. One extracts the small machine, the host
machine with a register for every whole number, the host with PAY, both universal programs $U$ and
$U_P$ written out instruction by instruction, and the loaders. The other extracts the compiler below
and its runner.

separately from the same specification. Both implement the small machine, the host with a
register for every whole number, the host with PAY, the universal programs and the loaders.

Two things about that build are worth knowing before you believe a word of the rest. First, the functions
supplied to extraction are the ones the theorems describe. Coq won't extract some of the files directly (a
technical limit on files that rename modules), so the extracted functions are copies with plain
names, and each copy is proved equal to the original, by computation or by a short proof, inside Coq.
The two universal programs are printed by Coq as literal lists and proved equal to the programs in
the theorems.

Second, whole numbers, and here my first instinct was the wrong one. The quick way to build is to map
Coq's whole numbers onto the computer's own machine integers, which are fast. They're 63 bits wide
here, and the guest codes $U$ reads go up near $2^{100}$, so they'd wrap around without a
word of warning. Coq's whole numbers never overflow. A machine word does, and the book already told
you what that cost Ariane 5 (\hyperref[sec:straight]{Let me be straight with you}). So the extraction maps Coq's whole numbers
to an OCaml library of unbounded integers, and each arithmetic operation is mapped by hand to that
library's version of it. Those are the hand-written substitutions in the trusted path: one line
that maps Coq's whole numbers onto the library's integers, a few that map Coq's Booleans,
decisions, lists, pairs, options and its one-value type onto OCaml's own, two that map Coq's
``and'' and ``or'' onto OCaml's, two in one file that map the hosts' one-value property types onto
OCaml's unit, and the arithmetic operations, seventeen in one file and
thirteen in the other. Each arithmetic line carries a one-line justification next to it: addition is addition, subtraction stops at zero the way Coq's does, division by zero gives
zero the way Coq's does. The rest is Coq's own definitions. The hand-written code outside that is two
drivers, which read input, print output, and count steps while they call the extracted step function
in a loop.

codes $U$ reads go up near $2^{100}$, so ordinary fixed-width arithmetic would wrap around.

integers, with arithmetic chosen to match the definitions: subtraction stops at zero and
division by zero returns zero. The mappings, compilers and input/output routines remain
implementation dependencies; testing them does not change the mathematical definitions.

\begin{theorem}[The compiler is correct]\label{thm:running-compiler}
For every source program with no recursion, and every input: the program computes $y$ exactly when
the runner (the Coq function that gets extracted) halts with $y$ for some amount of fuel; exactly when the compiled host program
halts with $y$; exactly when the two-counter guest halts with $y$; and exactly when $U_P$ running that
guest halts with $y$, with its first counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So compiling
a program computes its answer and certifies nothing: the compiler is a route to answers, and a
certification has to be written into the source as a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The runner also
takes exactly as many steps as the host program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run
that doesn't halt has used all its fuel.
\end{theorem}

The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
\emph{products}, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its two four-body entries are tied, one the negative of the other. That tie is a
constraint, $\langle \{A_0, A_1\} \otimes \{B_0, B_1\} \rangle = 0$: the zero entries of the first
rung don't imply it, and a classical strategy breaks it (\code{q1ab\_tie\_is\_a\_constraint},
QuantumPartitionPSD\_\allowbreak{}1AB.v). So the second rung is level 1+AB on that slice, and
that's what I mean by level 1+AB everywhere in this book. Its PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition.
The check for it proves something stronger, that the matrix is positive definite, by a cascade of
two Schur steps down to a four-by-four that Sylvester's criterion closes.
Sylvester's name on a test about matrices fits in a way I enjoy, because the word
\emph{matrix} is his. In 1850, in the \emph{Philosophical Magazine}, the English
mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used it for an ``oblong arrangement of
terms'' out of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and \emph{matrix} was
already an old word for the place something grows from. That's exactly what the test does:
it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two, three, four (the
leading minors), and asks each one's determinant to be positive. Was he the first to state the
test? The name doesn't settle that; names stick to people for all kinds of reasons, and I'd
treat this one as a lead.
And a fact that's easy to list without noticing what it means: with all five extra numbers at
zero, the condition certifies a strict \emph{subset of the classical set} (the ball where the four
correlators' squares sum to at most one), forcing S at most two
; it can't certify anything above the
classical line. To get a point above two you have to supply the extras
(\code{q1ab\_certifies\_a\_superclassical\_chsh\_point}, S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one
half). Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation} has the algebra.

The completion set is inside the quantum tables. This is Tsirelson's representation, and the
construction is his. Take a table with a PSD completion. A PSD matrix is a table of inner
products of vectors, always: peel off one row at a time, and a zero on the diagonal forces its
whole row to zero. So the completion hands over four unit vectors in four
dimensions, $a_0, a_1$ for Alice and $b_0, b_1$ for Bob, with $a_x \cdot b_y$ equal to the table's
entries. Now the trick. There are four real eight-by-eight matrices, built from the two-by-two ones that swap
two entries or flip the sign of one, that each square to the identity and anticommute in pairs:
multiply any two of them in either order and the answers differ only in sign
(\code{tr\_gamma\_clifford}, checked by computation). Use a vector's four components to mix
those four matrices, and you get an observable that squares to the identity, a legitimate
measurement. Give Alice and Bob a maximally entangled pair of eight-level systems, and the
correlator of two such observables comes out as exactly the inner product of their vectors
. So the strategy built from the four vectors produces the table
(\code{tr\_representation} for real amplitudes and \code{tr\_representation\_complex} for complex,
TsirelsonRepresentation.v). Eight levels on each side is always enough.

\emph{Borrowed, with names.} As the opening chapter warned, I usually had the hunch first and
found these names after, and that order doesn't make any of it mine. Everything in Part I (every
source is cited where it's used), the category theory (Eilenberg, Mac Lane) included. Minsky's
two-counter machines and the Coq library that proves their halting undecidable and compiles
computable functions into them (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the
diagonal pattern, Lawvere's unification, and the mechanized versions of them:
Michael Norrish's in HOL4, Mario Carneiro's in
Lean, and Yannick Forster, Fabian Kunze and Gert Smolka's in Coq. Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Stephanie Wehner's semidefinite proof of Tsirelson's bound (2006), NPA, Landau,
Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and the machine-checked proofs of Tsirelson's bound that came
before mine (Echenim and Mhalla in Isabelle, and Lean's mathlib). Landauer, Bennett, Szilard,
Maxwell, and their critics. The potential method (Tarjan) and its mechanizations (Nipkow,
Charguéraud and Pottier), Lamport's clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley,
Shannon, Rissanen. Zurek. The guarantee about every program: the reference monitor (Anderson),
execution monitors (Schneider), and monitors checked at every instruction and verified in Coq
(Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors). The counting under the permanence results: Poincaré's
recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4 and CompCert discipline. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer's own example and Shannon's
bounds, and ``set a bit to one whatever it held'' is my way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.

\emph{Who it's safe against.} Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one writer
stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It doesn't cover whoever
sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts nobody checked), a reset or a
power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire that carries the report, someone who
flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step, or a second writer that changes a
counter without bumping its edition. Those are the operator, the device and the tool chain,
and they're outside this fence. A record read by someone who didn't watch it being made is only
as good as their reason to believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote
over measured state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section~\ref{sec:windows} and
Section~\ref{sec:models}, and this book builds neither.
What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no program forges the chain. Availability is
a different promise, and it isn't given. A hostile program can put the trap up or fill the table,
and after that nothing useful gets done. The proofs also use Coq's whole numbers, which never
overflow, so versions and the ledger grow without bound. A build with fixed-width counters,
versions or ledger has to stop before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up, because a
wrapped version could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped ledger would fall.
Starting, restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the implementation, and none of
them is proved here.

\emph{The machine.} Part IV has one small machine, with the hosts that run it,
and here's its fence. The small machine of
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} (two counters, six instruction kinds) is where commitments are
earned: from a clean start, a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the
same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest such run adds exactly three to the ledger, a price reached
by a check that could have failed (the step doesn't police trivial checks: a check that can't
fail certifies for three too). It's also
where universality is proved, by matching Minsky's two-counter machines step for step and
borrowing their undecidable halting from the Coq library. It's Thiele-complete under a
definition every clock-style machine fails, and every machine meeting that definition hides its
record and ledger from its own window. The universal Thiele machine is one fixed program, $U$,
on a host with the small machine's instruction kinds and more counters, with no guest step built
in: it runs every program of the small machine from every clean start $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$, halts when the guest halts, raises
its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and only if the guest's flag rises somewhere in the guest's run,
and keeps a ledger equal to the guest's at every matching point. With one paid move added, one
fixed program, $U_P$, runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and
reading computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver. The
host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest's reading, raised on its own
earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest's plus a surcharge of at
most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies
with its whole ledger below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler
host with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest's
flag; its ledger only covers the guest's. The small machine's check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen,
and its certificate is historical (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} lists the rest).

\emph{The comparison machines.} The small machines I built to compare against are fragments too.
The random-access memory result covers an addressed list memory with load, increment and
decrement on cells (\code{concrete\_ram\_write\_reads\_back} and its neighbours), and it's about that
machine. The register machine Section~\ref{sec:latch} puts the latch on  is
a different small machine, the one with indirect addressing, and that theorem is about it. The reversible-machine
result covers arithmetic update cores: add and subtract, each undone by the other, with or
without wrapping at a modulus.
None is a theorem about real memories or full reversible languages. The cost-semantics
results are local correspondences, short of full cost-framework embeddings: the trace's cost is a
writer cost and a grade, and the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
Nobody's whole type system gets embedded either.

before:
If you asked what's new here, I wouldn't give you one thing, because there isn't one. There
are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the toll isn't only my
preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only be turned on by a step that
merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges},
Observation~\ref{thm:toll-derived}). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the price on a merge is Landauer's, as a
premise. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on that merge for finite
automata, so what's here is the toll as a rule on a ledger. Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can't price the
raise exactly (Observation~\ref{thm:shadow-price}); that a price computed from what a window shows
can't tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and what's here is the
pricing form. Third, a record driven by the
computation that never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base
(Observation~\ref{thm:u11-latch}); latches and history variables are old, and the theorem covers
only records that never come down. Fourth, a record that's priced, and on the small machine
earned (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}), under the move of guaranteeing something about
every program. That move isn't mine at all. It's the reference monitor's (Anderson, 1972),
made precise for monitors that watch a run (Schneider, 2000), and verified in Coq for monitors
checked at every instruction (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What's put together under
it here is built and checked, and its idea isn't new: the check bound to the edition it looked
at, the toll paid on top, and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small
machine and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} sorts all four with sources.

``Kernel'' wears three hats in this book, so here they are before one of them ambushes
you. First, mathematics: the kernel of a map is what it sends to the identity, and for a
projection the useful version is the relation ``these two states project to the same thing.''
Second, the proofs, where the hat comes in two sizes: the kernel tier, the part of the Coq
development where the model is written down and its main theorems live (Section~\ref{sec:coq}),
with the link files that tie the small machine to them;
and Coq's own kernel, the small checker that accepts or rejects every proof. Third, the
operating-system kernel, the core of an operating system, as in the packet-filter example
in Section~\ref{sec:models}. The
sentence around the word always says which one is.
after:
``Kernel'' has two uses here. In mathematics, the kernel of a map is what it sends to the
identity; for a projection the useful version is the relation ``these two states project
to the same thing.'' An operating-system kernel is the core of an operating system, as in
the packet-filter example in Section~\ref{sec:models}.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936, who essentially proved it without stating it in
this form; Stephen Kleene stated it in 1952, and Martin Davis seems to have been the first to name it, in 1958,
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}): no program decides, for every program and input,
whether it stops. Kleene's recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for any transformation
of programs that can itself be computed, some program behaves exactly like its own
transform. Rice's theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that depends only on what a
program does, and isn't true of all programs or of none, can't be decided by a program. The
diagonal is the move under all three: build the thing that does the opposite of what the
table says about it (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). L is a small lambda calculus, a language made of nothing but
functions applied to functions, which Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka built in Coq and which
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} uses as a tool. A hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so
that finding two inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds
each new record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into
one root (Section~\ref{sec:toll}, Section~\ref{sec:models}).
